practiceQuestions.stem: An infant born at 29 weeks has increased work of breathing shortly after birth. Which response best reflects an examination-level reasoning approach?

options.text: Assume classic RDS and select a treatment from memory.
Use gestational age, trajectory, exam and available studies to compare RDS with other causes; current decisions follow supervised local protocol.
Exclude infection because symptoms are early.
Use oxygen requirement alone to establish the diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Prematurity makes surfactant deficiency plausible but not pathognomonic. The ABP blueprint tests core science and diagnosis/monitoring; differential, trend, and test limits matter. No specific treatment is prescribed here.

practiceQuestions.stem: A preterm newborn has hypoxemia and labile oxygenation with suspected elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Which concept is most important?

options.text: A single saturation reading establishes persistent pulmonary hypertension.
Consider transitional physiology, shunt direction and cardiopulmonary assessment together; seek supervised expert evaluation.
Pulmonary hypertension can be excluded if an initial film is normal.
A single biomarker is confirmatory.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A single observation is insufficient. The blueprint includes pulmonary hypertension and cardiovascular physiology; hemodynamic evaluation is contextual and requires clinical expertise.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn with perinatal compromise develops abnormal movements. What best describes the next educational reasoning step?

options.text: Label all abnormal movements as seizures.
Distinguish clinical observation from electrographic confirmation and consider differential, timing, and monitoring limitations.
Assume hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy based on movements alone.
Ignore gestational age when interpreting neurologic findings.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The outline includes neurologic examination, neonatal seizures, and HIE. Observation alone is not definitive and should prompt appropriate supervised assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes an early-onset infection risk framework?

options.text: Maternal risk factors alone prove neonatal infection.
Use maternal/perinatal context, infant signs, appropriate tests, and the current local guideline; balance missed disease against unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.
A reassuring initial appearance rules out later deterioration.
Any respiratory distress requires identical management regardless of context.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABP domain covers infection and stewardship; risk assessment is probabilistic, contextual, and updated with clinical evolution.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which evidence task is most appropriate when reviewing a neonatal nutrition study?

options.text: Accept author conclusion without checking population.
Check gestational-age/population, intervention, comparator, outcomes, harms and applicability before translating findings.
Assume a growth percentile change proves a treatment effect.
Convert a research result into a patient-specific feeding order.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Critical appraisal and population applicability are core evidence tasks. An independent course does not provide clinical authority.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 34-week infant has jaundice. Which is true about the AAP 2022 hyperbilirubinemia guideline?

options.text: It directly sets its routine thresholds for all infants below 35 weeks.
Its scope is newborns of 35 or more weeks; a 34-week infant requires a different evidence/protocol pathway.
It is a universal diagnosis tool for cholestasis.
It removes the need to consider age in hours.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP describes the 2022 guideline for infants ≥35 weeks gestation; applying it below that population boundary is not supported by its stated scope. Check current local neonatal references.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a resuscitation exam question, which statement is safest?

options.text: A recorded lecture confers neonatal resuscitation certification.
Use the currently effective AHA/AAP guideline as a study source; real resuscitation requires trained team practice and current institutional protocols.
A study guide replaces hands-on NRP training.
One algorithm applies without regard to the infant and context.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guidelines support learning, but competence requires approved training, hands-on practice, and clinical supervision. This self-study has no certification/competence effect.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn has multiple congenital anomalies. What is an appropriate genetics-learning response?

options.text: Infer one named syndrome from one nonspecific feature.
Build a differential and identify family history, phenotype, consent, and potential testing questions for specialist discussion.
Assume a negative screening result excludes all genetic conditions.
Order testing using a course as authorization.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABP outline includes common chromosome, single-gene, and syndromic disease. Phenotype-guided differential and consultation avoid overclaiming.

practiceQuestions.stem: An extremely preterm infant has an unexpected glucose trend. Which approach best reflects the blueprint?

options.text: Interpret one measurement without sampling context.
Verify specimen/time/trajectory and physiologic context, consider a differential, and seek supervised evaluation.
Assume all hypoglycemia is due to prematurity.
Use an educational case report as a dosing protocol.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Endocrine/metabolic knowledge includes normal physiology and disorders; interpreting trend and context is essential. No treatment advice is supplied.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a neonatal case report with clinical images, what is permissible in this course?

options.text: Copy image files because the article is free to read.
Link to the authentic article; reuse only if the license permits, with attribution and required context, and never upload patient data.
Assume de-identified means unrestricted reuse.
Remove the citation to protect privacy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view is not blanket reuse permission. The linked Frontiers report states CC BY and written guardian consent for potentially identifiable images/data; any reuse still requires attribution and license compliance.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the correct interpretation of ABP neonatal-perinatal certification eligibility?

options.text: Finishing this online course fulfills the three-year fellowship requirement.

Ordinary ABP admission requires three full-time years in an ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited program plus prerequisite general pediatrics certification, unrestricted license, verified competence/scholarship, and passing exam.
An in-training score grants subspecialty certification.
Research-only fellowship guarantees eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP identifies a separate certifying exam and requires formal accredited fellowship, general pediatrics certification/maintenance, licensure, program verification, scholarly activity and passing exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: What makes a neonatal QI aim useful for a course assignment?

options.text: It promises a clinical outcome without baseline data.
It specifies a process/population/timeframe, a measurable outcome and balancing measure, and safeguards/equity context.
It claims an online proposal meets ABP scholarship requirements.
It omits stakeholder involvement.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Harvard fellowship QI curriculum includes systems thinking, measurement, patient safety, and a project; ABP scholarship is a separate training requirement with work product and local oversight.

title: Neonatal-Perinatal Medicine Training Programs
prerequisites: Completed medical degree and general pediatrics residency for clinical fellowship context; ABP eligibility is governed by ABP rules, not this course.
Foundational physiology, pharmacology, microbiology, statistics, and clinical examination knowledge.
This course is advanced self-study, not an entry-level qualification or patient-care authorization.
objectives: Map fetal, maternal, delivery and neonatal factors to a structured differential.
Reason across the ABP’s 17 content domains and four universal tasks: core science; risk assessment; diagnosis/testing/monitoring; management/treatment/prevention.
Interpret evidence and acknowledge uncertainty, confounding and limits of individual tests.
Discuss stabilization, respiratory/cardiovascular support, infection, nutrition, neurologic outcomes, multisystem disease, systems care, family partnership and QI at a conceptual level.
Use lawful public clinical references and preserve patient privacy and image rights.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a newborn with persistent respiratory distress after initial stabilization, which approach best avoids premature closure?

options.text: Assume respiratory distress syndrome based on prematurity alone
Integrate history, examination, and radiographic/laboratory evidence while considering pulmonary and nonpulmonary causes
Order broad genetic sequencing before reassessment
Treat tachypnea alone as proof of pneumonia

practiceQuestions.rationale: A broad differential is needed; history, exam and investigations help tailor diagnosis, and causes may be outside the lungs.

practiceQuestions.stem: A neonatal sepsis review describes blood culture as the reference standard. What is the most defensible interpretation of a negative culture?

options.text: It excludes all infection
It must be interpreted with clinical context and culture limitations; it does not automatically settle suspected infection
It proves a viral cause
It requires antibiotics for a fixed five days in all circumstances

practiceQuestions.rationale: The review describes culture as the gold standard but notes diagnostic uncertainty; decisions depend on context and reassessment, not a universal duration.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which body sets the US subspecialty certification process described for Neonatal-Perinatal Medicine?

options.text: American Board of Pediatrics
ACGME
NRMP
AAP Section on Neonatal-Perinatal Medicine

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP establishes the subspecialty certification requirements and examination; ACGME accredits training programs.

practiceQuestions.stem: According to ABP published eligibility criteria accessed for this course, the standard fellowship duration is:

options.text: One year
Two years
Three years full-time in an ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited program
A short online course

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP states three years of full-time broad-based training in an ACGME-accredited US or RCPSC-accredited Canadian program.

topicGaps: Only 7.684 unique, free, accessible hours are verified from observed recording durations; the 36.0h floor still has an actual 28.316h gap. Existing and newly authored target minutes are not rendered video hours.

No publicly inspectable complete Boston Children’s fellowship didactic/rotation schedule or official pediatric-specific Addiction Medicine board blueprint was identified; the published ABPM Addiction Medicine outline maps general board domains, not this pediatric-focused track.

Coverage remains incomplete for detailed, current age/product-specific MOUD prescribing, supervised withdrawal/intoxication management, acute toxicology, pediatric substance-specific pharmacotherapy, and longitudinal clinical decision-making; online self-study cannot substitute for observed supervised care.

Non-opioid substance classes are introduced by a linked 2026 Maine AAP session and older overview recordings, but depth for alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, sedatives, stimulants, hallucinogens, dissociatives, inhalants, anabolic steroids, other substances, and nonsubstance addictions is not sufficient to treat the published ABPM outline as comprehensively taught.

Several accessible recordings date to 2021 and may use historical population estimates, tool versions, and evidence; current surveillance, validated-tool versions, labeling, and clinical guidance must be checked before educational or clinical reuse.
Minor consent, privacy, mandatory reporting, emergency protocols, and local referral requirements remain jurisdiction-specific; no qualified local legal or human clinical review was performed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (pediatric-focused Addiction Medicine; not a separately boarded pediatric subspecialty)
boardNames: American Board of Preventive Medicine (ABPM) — Addiction Medicine subspecialty certification; no separate Pediatric Addiction Medicine board examination identified
medical.boardStatus: ABPM lists Addiction Medicine as a subspecialty certification. Its published Addiction Medicine outline covers general addiction medicine; no separate pediatric addiction medicine examination or pediatric-specific exam blueprint was found in the current official ABPM materials checked. ACGME accreditation of the institutional fellowship is a separate matter from board certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABPM’s current ACGME-fellowship pathway requires 12 months or more in an ACGME-accredited Addiction Medicine fellowship and current primary specialty certification through an eligible board. The institutional listing says this one-year clinical fellowship is ACGME-accredited, but independent self-study confers no fellowship completion, eligibility determination, examination access or certification. Confirm current rules directly with ABPM and the relevant primary board.

Non-opioid substance classes are introduced by a linked 2026 Maine AAP session and older overview recordings, but depth for alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, sedatives, stimulants, hallucinogens, dissociatives, inhalants, anabolic steroids, other substances, and nonsubstance addictions is not sufficient to treat the published ABPM outline as comprehensively taught.

Several accessible recordings date to 2021 and may use historical population estimates, tool versions, and evidence; current surveillance, validated-tool versions, labeling, and clinical guidance must be checked before educational or clinical reuse.
Minor consent, privacy, mandatory reporting, emergency protocols, and local referral requirements remain jurisdiction-specific; no qualified local legal or human clinical review was performed.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 15-year-old completes an adolescent substance-use screener with a positive result. What is the most defensible next step?

options.text: Record a substance-use disorder diagnosis solely from the score.
Use the result to guide a confidential, developmentally appropriate follow-up assessment and risk discussion.
Order a urine drug screen as a diagnostic confirmation before speaking with the adolescent.
Immediately disclose the result to every caregiver regardless of risk or local law.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screeners identify risk and guide further assessment; they are not diagnoses. Confidentiality limits and any caregiver involvement require a safety- and jurisdiction-aware approach. Toxicology does not replace history.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes what an adolescent screening tool can establish?

options.text: A positive score establishes DSM-5-TR SUD severity.
A positive score establishes the exact substance used.
A screening result stratifies concern and informs what assessment or brief response may follow.
A negative result rules out all future or undisclosed substance use.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAP and NIDA describe validated tools as screening/triage aids, not definitive diagnosis or toxicological identification.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a routine visit, a teen asks whether everything they say will remain secret. Which response is best?

options.text: “Yes, absolutely; nothing will ever be shared.”
Explain the practice’s privacy policy and relevant limits, including safety and local law, before continuing.
Avoid discussing confidentiality and begin screening.
Tell the teen that parents are always entitled to every detail.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP and SAMHSA recommend making privacy arrangements and limits clear; confidentiality is not absolute and minor-consent law varies.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adolescent describes regular use but reports no acute symptoms. What is the best educational conclusion from the screen alone?

options.text: There is no clinical risk because the adolescent is asymptomatic today.
A positive screen warrants clarifying pattern, consequences, functioning, co-occurrence, strengths and safety before determining next steps.
A diagnosis is certain if the youth admits any use.
A urine test is sufficient to determine severity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Assessment is broader than frequency alone and includes developmental/biopsychosocial context. A screen, current appearance, or toxicology result alone is insufficient.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teen with possible opioid use disorder says they will not attend therapy. Which general statement is most consistent with the current AAP youth opioid resource?

options.text: Medication should be withheld until the teen completes therapy.
Behavioral care may be offered when indicated, but therapy should not be a prerequisite to medication treatment.
Medication treatment is inappropriate for adolescents.
A screening result alone specifies which medication and dose to use.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP’s public FAQ states medication treatment should not be contingent on therapy; actual treatment decisions require current clinical assessment and qualified care.
practiceQuestions.domain: Pharmacologic and behavioral treatment; adolescent OUD

practiceQuestions.stem: A peer reports that an adolescent may have overdosed after using an unknown pill. What should the learning objective prioritize?

options.text: Debate whether the teen meets SUD criteria before acting.
Prioritize immediate emergency response and applicable overdose-reversal guidance, with clinical assessment after stabilization.
Use the pill’s appearance to identify its contents.
Wait for a definitive toxicology result before obtaining urgent help.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Possible overdose is an acute safety problem; counterfeit pills and unknown exposures cannot be reliably identified by appearance or delayed testing. Seek emergency response and follow current local protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is a sound teaching use of an adolescent case vignette?

options.text: Assume the vignette’s diagnosis and treatment generalize to every similar-age patient.
Separate case facts from unknowns, check the linked source’s provenance, and discuss limits of generalization.
Rehost its images and transcript because the case is public.
Treat an illustrative case as a substitute for a guideline.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Case reports/teaching vignettes illustrate reasoning but cannot establish universal practice; the source’s patient authenticity/consent or reuse license must not be assumed.
practiceQuestions.domain: Evidence appraisal; ethics and lawful educational use

practiceQuestions.stem: A youth’s urine immunoassay is positive for one drug class. What conclusion is most appropriate before changing care?

options.text: The result definitively identifies a specific drug and proves impairment.
Interpret the result in clinical context, with assay limitations and confirmatory testing as appropriate; continue history and assessment.
The result alone establishes DSM severity.
A negative result would exclude all substance exposure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening assays have limitations and cannot alone determine exact exposure, timing, impairment or diagnosis. The course requires context and qualified interpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which board-content statement is accurate for this course?

options.text: ABPM publishes a separate Pediatric Addiction Medicine exam blueprint.
The ABPM Addiction Medicine outline is the relevant published board outline; no separate pediatric addiction medicine exam was identified.
The Boston Children’s fellowship itself guarantees board eligibility and certification.
A free online course is equivalent to accredited fellowship training.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPM publishes Addiction Medicine subspecialty content/eligibility information. We found no separate pediatric addiction exam. Completion of an independent course does not satisfy board or fellowship requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: A student proposes concluding that an adolescent’s cannabis use caused their depressed mood because both are present. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Accept the causal claim because co-occurrence proves direction.
Assess both conditions and their timeline, safety, function and context; avoid inferring causation from co-occurrence alone.
Ignore mood symptoms until substance use stops.
Classify the patient without further assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Co-occurring symptoms require integrated assessment; temporal and clinical context matters. Neither a screening result nor association establishes causation.

title: Pediatric Anesthesiology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent, non-accredited self-study curriculum)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate physician self-study, designed for learners who have completed anesthesiology residency or are undertaking a supervised pediatric anesthesiology fellowship; it is not an entry-level anesthesia or patient-care course.
knowledge: Medical-school physiology, pharmacology, pediatric developmental principles and core anesthesiology knowledge.
Working understanding of anesthesia monitoring and perioperative team roles.
Ability to read board outlines and primary references critically.
prerequisites.practiceLimits: No patient care, prescriptions, credentialing, procedural demonstrations, unsupervised practice or hands-on skill assessment. Clinical learners must follow their institution and supervising clinician.

objectives: Map pediatric anesthesia reasoning to the ABA five-section pediatric subspecialty outline and SPA learning goals.
Synthesize developmental physiology, age-related pharmacology and equipment considerations at a conceptual level.
Use a structured, family-centered preoperative assessment and recognize when consultation/escalation is needed.
Reason across airway/respiratory, neonatal, cardiovascular, neurologic, surgical-organ-system, regional/pain, PACU/NORA and safety topics.
Evaluate claims using current authoritative sources and distinguish board blueprint, ACGME standards, institution-specific curriculum and local clinical policy.
Communicate uncertainty, privacy, equity, informed consent and patient-safety considerations.

units.title: Developmental anatomy, physiology, pharmacology and equipment
objectives: Compare age-related changes in airway, respiratory mechanics, circulation, body water and thermoregulation without treating age bands as a substitute for individual assessment.
Explain developmental pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic differences and how monitoring/equipment choices interact with size and physiology.
Interpret basic ventilator, gas, oxygenation, temperature and neuromuscular-monitor signals at the conceptual level.
topics: Airway and developmental anatomy; respiratory/circulatory transition; pediatric pharmacology; circuits and monitors; ultrasound fundamentals.
boardDomains: II organ-based basic and clinical sciences
units.casePractice: Fictional age-stratified physiologic comparison: identify which assumptions do not transfer across an infant, school-age child and adolescent.
units.assessment: Annotated concept map and five-item retrieval quiz; explain uncertainty and where a current drug reference is required.

units.title: Preoperative assessment, family-centered care and preparation
objectives: Structure history/exam and risk review around age, coexisting disease, airway, prior anesthesia, medications, fasting history and planned procedure.
Identify communication, assent/consent, language access, disability and family priorities that change the plan.
Distinguish elective optimization from urgent care; document reasons to seek additional expertise.
topics: Development and comorbidities; URI/reactive airway disease; OSA/obesity; neurodiversity; informed consent and shared decision-making; fasting guidelines as current local policy.
boardDomains: V B/E professionalism, ethics and disparities
units.casePractice: Fictional pre-op consult worksheet with a child who communicates differently and a caregiver needing an interpreter; no diagnosis presumed from a label.
units.assessment: Structured oral presentation scored for risk factors, family communication, limits and escalation plan.

units.title: Airway, respiratory disease and perioperative respiratory events
objectives: Construct a pediatric airway and respiratory risk differential before induction, including age, airway phenotype, infection, aspiration and procedural context.
Compare oxygenation/ventilation observations and identify when trends, waveform quality or clinical context make an apparent value unreliable.
Describe a team-based difficult-airway preparation and escalation at a principles level; do not treat a short video as procedural credentialing.
topics: Mask ventilation and tracheal intubation principles; difficult airway; upper/lower airway disease; foreign body/ENT; OSA; extubation and respiratory complications.
boardDomains: IV A/D/E/G general anesthesia and complications
units.casePractice: Use a fictional airway briefing to identify primary/backup oxygenation strategy, equipment checks, help triggers and post-event debrief topics.
units.assessment: Written airway-risk synthesis and simulation observation checklist; this is not assessment of hands-on competence.

units.title: Neonatal, infant and premature patient anesthesia
objectives: Relate post-conceptional age, prematurity, comorbid respiratory disease and surgical urgency to perioperative planning questions.
Organize a neonatal case review around thermoregulation, glucose/fluid/blood planning, oxygenation, transport and postoperative destination.
Differentiate common neonatal surgical problems and their physiologic implications while avoiding single-sign diagnostic certainty.
topics: Neonatal physiology; apnea/bradycardia; congenital diaphragmatic hernia; TEF; gastroschisis/omphalocele; pyloric stenosis; NEC; neonatal resuscitation and transport.
units.casePractice: Fictional neonatal handoff worksheet: list missing information, stabilization responsibilities, destination, and the interprofessional team to involve.
units.assessment: Concept map and handoff grading: physiologic relevance, contingency clarity, and explicit uncertainty.

units.title: Congenital heart disease, cardiovascular physiology and cardiac procedures
objectives: Describe fetal/transitional circulation and relate lesion physiology, prior palliation/repair, ventricular function and pulmonary hypertension to the anesthetic question set.
Differentiate cardiac anesthesia for cardiac versus non-cardiac surgery and identify consultation/monitoring decisions for expert teams.
Explain broad bypass, arrhythmia and transplant issues without providing unsupervised procedural direction.
topics: Acyanotic/cyanotic lesions; single-ventricle physiology; pulmonary hypertension; cardiomyopathy; CPB; cath/electrophysiology; noncardiac surgery in CHD.
boardDomains: III C and F clinical procedural subspecialties
units.casePractice: Fictional lesion-physiology matrix: label knowns, unknowns, hemodynamic threats, and which congenital-cardiac anesthesiology consult is needed.
units.assessment: Oral reasoning rubric: physiology first, evidence quality, safe escalation, no unsupported drug/dose prescription.

units.title: Regional anesthesia, acute pain and chronic pain in children
objectives: Compare neuraxial and peripheral regional options at a conceptual level with indication, contraindication, consent, monitoring and rescue context.
Explain developmental pain, multimodal analgesia, opioid stewardship, local-anesthetic systemic toxicity recognition and chronic pain-team collaboration.
Use evidence cautiously when translating procedure videos to an individual patient; no unsupervised block practice.
topics: Caudal/epidural/spinal; peripheral blocks and ultrasound; acute postoperative and chronic pain; nonpharmacologic approaches; palliative care; SUD recognition.
units.casePractice: Fictional pain conference referral: specify family goals, age-appropriate assessment, competing risks and a supervised team review.
units.assessment: Short evidence appraisal and risk/benefit matrix; procedural skill is not evaluated or authorized.

units.title: Neurosurgery, neurologic disease, imaging and neurodisability
objectives: Relate intracranial pressure, seizure history, neurologic baseline and procedure to a preoperative plan and postoperative assessment needs.
Recognize neurodivergent communication/sensory needs and adapt preparation collaboratively without assuming incapacity.
Identify multimorbidity and uncertainty requiring specialty consultation.
topics: Hydrocephalus; tumors; seizures; traumatic brain injury; spinal disorders; neuromuscular conditions; neuroimaging; developmental disability and autism.
units.casePractice: Fictional child with a communication aid and planned imaging: produce a sensory-sensitive workflow and handoff, while preserving assent/consent and safety.
units.assessment: Reflective plan scored for individualized language, safety and respect for patient/family priorities.

units.title: ENT, craniofacial, ophthalmic and airway surgery
objectives: Connect anatomy, surgical access, shared airway, bleeding and postoperative obstruction risks with a team briefing.
Identify relevant comorbid OSA, craniofacial variation and prior airway history; consider procedure-specific recovery needs.
Explain why a single airway examination or video clip cannot certify competence.
topics: Tonsil/adenoid; tracheostomy; bronchoscopy; laryngotracheal reconstruction; craniosynostosis/cleft; ophthalmic/strabismus; shared airway and extubation.
units.casePractice: Fictional multidisciplinary shared-airway huddle with surgeon and recovery team; learners mark decision points and unresolved contingencies.
units.assessment: Case conference scorecard for anatomy, communication, airway risk, plan B and disposition.

units.title: Gastrointestinal, genitourinary, endocrine and metabolic disease
objectives: Recognize common pediatric surgical disease states in the ABA outline and name anesthetic-relevant physiology without extrapolating beyond source.
Relate adrenal/thyroid/diabetes/electrolyte disease and obesity to preoperative assessment, consultation and recovery planning.
Identify fasting, aspiration and glycemic questions that require up-to-date policy-specific references.
topics: Pyloric stenosis; intestinal obstruction; NEC; transplant; renal disease; diabetes; adrenal insufficiency; thyroid disease; metabolic syndromes; obesity.
units.casePractice: Fictional pre-op problem list for child with endocrine history and planned surgery; distinguish stable facts from missing labs/policy questions.
units.assessment: Source-referenced plan with correct escalation and no invented dosing.

units.title: Hematology, oncology, transplantation, trauma and burns
objectives: Organize pediatric transfusion/blood conservation decisions around patient-specific risks and institutional protocols.
Recognize implications of chemotherapy, immune compromise, coagulopathy, trauma, burns and transplantation for perioperative assessment.
Separate evidence-based thresholds from local decision authority.
topics: Anemia/coagulation; oncology therapies; stem cell/organ transplant; blood management; pediatric trauma/abuse concerns; burns/inhalation injury.
units.casePractice: Fictional oncology case conference: identify questions for hematology/oncology and blood bank; protect privacy and avoid treatment orders.
units.assessment: Evidence-linked transfusion-risk memo, graded on contextual reasoning and limits.

units.title: Post-anesthesia care, critical care, NORA and crisis management
objectives: Construct a postoperative monitoring/disposition rationale based on illness, operation, recovery trajectory and locally agreed resources.
Discuss pediatric sedation, remote-area planning, rescue readiness, crisis resource management and closed-loop team communication.
Analyze a near miss using system factors and a learning-focused debrief rather than individual blame.
topics: PACU; PICU/NICU; sedation/MAC; NORA/radiology; ECMO; transport; perioperative crisis; QI and human factors.
boardDomains: IV E/F/G/H; V G quality and safety
units.casePractice: Fictional simulation storyboard using a crisis cognitive aid. Learner names role assignments, call-for-help threshold, checklist use and debrief questions.
units.assessment: Scenario reasoning rubric: situational awareness, communication, escalation and systems improvement; no real patient record.

units.title: Professionalism, evidence, quality, ethics and disparities
objectives: Evaluate an educational claim by source type/date and distinguish guideline, blueprint, accreditation standard and local policy.
Apply consent, privacy, disclosure, human-factors, equity, access and communication principles to pediatric care.
Develop a small, measurable QI question without claiming causal benefit from an uncontrolled metric.
topics: Consent/assent; privacy; research ethics; disparities; limited-English access; clinical informatics; QI; safety metrics; lifelong learning.
boardDomains: V Professional issues, statistics, ethics, practice management, QI, DEI and disparities
units.casePractice: Fictional event review and QI proposal; no actual adverse event or patient data supplied.
units.assessment: Capstone: evidence audit, one-page case rationale, family communication plan, and QI measure with limitations.

assignment.title: Integrated fictional pediatric case conference and evidence audit
assignment.prompt: Choose one fully fictional case archetype from a unit. Submit a 1,000–1,500 word source-linked reasoning brief with pre-op information needs, patient/family communication, physiologic concerns, plan contingencies, team/escalation needs, postoperative questions, and 3–5 source classifications (board blueprint, ACGME requirement, guideline/review, institutional page). Do not include identifiable data or patient images, clinical orders or procedural steps.
assignment.passingUse: Formative course feedback only; not a validated test, credential, board predictor or practice evaluation.

components.name: Retrieval checks
components.method: Unit knowledge checks using original MCQs; feedback explains why alternatives fail.

components.name: Case reasoning worksheets
components.method: Fictional cases scored for evidence, uncertainty and safe consultation.

components.name: Assignments/capstone
components.method: Rubric above; faculty review is not provided.

components.name: Reflection/evidence audit
components.method: Distinguish accreditation, clinical guidance and local policy.

assessment.interpretation: Educational formative self-assessment only. Items are not ABA questions, not validated, and cannot predict passing.

studyHours.planRationale: A transparent 12-unit learning plan of approximately 10 study hours per unit: selected free recordings (5.41 observed hours), outline/readings, self-testing, fictional case worksheets, review and capstone. The plan is not a completed course log and does not imply equivalence to the 12-month ACGME fellowship. Actual reading/practice time varies.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine
mapping.name: Pediatric Anesthesiology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Packet preserves the exact institutional programme identity. The current department page [R4] identifies this as a 12-month ACGME-accredited physician fellowship (program 0422321028), with 28 weeks pediatric OR, four weeks pain, four weeks critical care elective among PICU/PCICU/NICU, 12 weeks cardiac OR/diagnostic laboratory in blocks, and CCPO exposure; rotation descriptions are this institution’s public curriculum, not national requirements. The page describes weekly didactics, scholarly activity and board preparation; its PassMachine course is not counted as free public media. A separate two-year non-ACGME fellowship is described for independent research and pediatric cardiac anesthesiology and is not conflated with the core 12-month ACGME track. Current department link: https://anesthesiology.hopkinsmedicine.org/pediatric-anesthesia/pediatric-anesthesia-fellowship/

mapping.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital
mapping.name: Pediatric Anesthesiology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The official BCH directory [R5] labels the core pediatric anesthesiology fellowship one year, ACGME-accredited, requiring anesthesiology residency; BCH describes separately organized advanced pediatric cardiac and pediatric regional offerings and a possible sequential two-year core-plus-advanced pathway. This is distinct from affiliated anesthesiology residency rotations at BCH and from its Pediatric Nurse Anesthesia Fellowship. Detailed independent curriculum and case logs were not publicly verified beyond the directory page; no specific volume or eligibility claim is inferred.

unitMap.text: Congenital heart disease, cardiovascular physiology and cardiac procedures
coveredTopics: Acyanotic/cyanotic lesions; single-ventricle physiology; pulmonary hypertension; cardiomyopathy; CPB; cath/electrophysiology; noncardiac surgery in CHD.

unitMap.text: Regional anesthesia, acute pain and chronic pain in children
coveredTopics: Caudal/epidural/spinal; peripheral blocks and ultrasound; acute postoperative and chronic pain; nonpharmacologic approaches; palliative care; SUD recognition.

unitMap.text: Neurosurgery, neurologic disease, imaging and neurodisability
coveredTopics: Hydrocephalus; tumors; seizures; traumatic brain injury; spinal disorders; neuromuscular conditions; neuroimaging; developmental disability and autism.

unitMap.text: ENT, craniofacial, ophthalmic and airway surgery
coveredTopics: Tonsil/adenoid; tracheostomy; bronchoscopy; laryngotracheal reconstruction; craniosynostosis/cleft; ophthalmic/strabismus; shared airway and extubation.

unitMap.text: Gastrointestinal, genitourinary, endocrine and metabolic disease
coveredTopics: Pyloric stenosis; intestinal obstruction; NEC; transplant; renal disease; diabetes; adrenal insufficiency; thyroid disease; metabolic syndromes; obesity.

unitMap.text: Hematology, oncology, transplantation, trauma and burns
coveredTopics: Anemia/coagulation; oncology therapies; stem cell/organ transplant; blood management; pediatric trauma/abuse concerns; burns/inhalation injury.

unitMap.text: Post-anesthesia care, critical care, NORA and crisis management
coveredTopics: PACU; PICU/NICU; sedation/MAC; NORA/radiology; ECMO; transport; perioperative crisis; QI and human factors.

unitMap.text: Professionalism, evidence, quality, ethics and disparities
coveredTopics: Consent/assent; privacy; research ethics; disparities; limited-English access; clinical informatics; QI; safety metrics; lifelong learning.

topicGaps: Verified, deduplicated accessible free recordings total 8.4736 hours against the 36-hour video target; the exact recording gap is 27.5264 hours. Authored scripts and clip-plan target minutes are not rendered media and add zero verified hours.

Public lecture coverage remains insufficient for developmental physiology/pharmacology, neonatal disease-specific anesthesia, detailed congenital-heart physiology and cardiac procedures, neurologic disease/neurosurgery, GI/GU and endocrine/metabolic disease, trauma/burns, oncology/transplant beyond blood management, and PACU/NORA/sedation/critical-care integration.
The new airway, regional/pain, blood-management and craniofacial recordings map to relevant units but do not replace practical teaching, local protocols, supervised cases or competency assessment.
Common-foundation teamwork, consent, quality, evidence and communication clips support selected objectives only; they are not pediatric disease instruction.

SPA Intensive Review material remains secured with no public free runtime verified; Hopkins PassMachine content is not public free media; APAGBI’s public video catalogue labels full access as a member benefit; scheduled grand-round event time is not a verified recording runtime. These items are excluded.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reviews a pediatric anesthesiology fellowship brochure and an ABA examination outline. Which statement best distinguishes their authority?

options.text: The brochure establishes the national exam blueprint.
The ABA outline describes exam content; a program page describes that institution’s offering, not a national blueprint.
The ACGME requirements grant individual board eligibility.
A course completion certificate grants clinical privileges.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABA publishes the subspecialty exam outline; institutional pages describe local training. ACGME accredits programs, while the certifying board sets its own eligibility and certification rules. Independent study grants neither eligibility nor privileges.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with a history of difficult airway and an upcoming procedure has no recent airway documentation. What is the best educational reasoning step?

options.text: Assume a normal airway because a prior anesthetic was completed.
Review prior records if lawfully available, examine the child, clarify procedure context and plan team escalation with current local resources.
Use a single internet video as procedural credentialing.
Proceed without documenting the uncertainty.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A thorough assessment integrates history, examination, prior events and procedure-specific context; uncertain or higher-risk cases need appropriate expert/team planning. The video in the course is brief educational material, not supervision or competency validation.
practiceQuestions.domain: IV A/D preoperative evaluation and airway

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about pediatric perioperative medication decisions is the most defensible?

options.text: A single fixed mg/kg value is appropriate regardless of age, indication, route or comorbidity.
Development affects pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics; verify an up-to-date authoritative reference and local protocol for an individual prescription.
Adult drug labels can always be linearly scaled by body weight.
A publicly available educational video constitutes a prescribing protocol.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABA outline specifically includes developmental pharmacology and physiological/pathophysiological states. This course provides conceptual learning, not dosing advice; patient-specific prescribing requires current references, context and qualified clinicians.

practiceQuestions.stem: A preterm infant with prior apnea is discussed for postoperative planning after anesthesia. Which reasoning frame is best?

options.text: Use one historical threshold as the only determinant of disposition.
Integrate maturity, comorbidities, current condition, procedure/anesthetic course, monitoring capacity and local policy with the responsible clinical team.
Assume all infants require identical management.
Ignore recovery trajectory if the operation was brief.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABA outline includes post-conceptional age, neonatal apnea/bradycardia, postoperative care and complications; individual planning is context-dependent and governed by current local policy and qualified teams.
practiceQuestions.domain: III B neonatal; IV G postoperative period

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional pediatric congenital-heart-disease pre-op discussion, which information is most important before reasoning about perioperative risk?

options.text: Only the lesion name.
Current physiology and functional status, prior repair/palliation, ventricular function, pulmonary vascular disease, planned procedure and specialist input.
A generic adult algorithm with no modification.
Assume all repaired lesions are physiologically normal.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The exam outline covers lesion physiology, palliative procedures, pulmonary hypertension, cardiac interventions and noncardiac procedures in children with CHD. A lesion label alone is insufficient; current physiology and expert input matter.
practiceQuestions.domain: II B cardiovascular; III cardiac clinical subspecialty

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description of the caudal epidural lecture is appropriate for this self-study course?

options.text: Completion certifies an independent learner to perform caudal blocks.
It is a free-to-view educational recording; procedural competence requires appropriate accredited training, supervision and assessment.
Its runtime is equivalent to fellowship case experience.
The video can be downloaded and inserted into a commercial course without permission.

practiceQuestions.rationale: An educational video can support conceptual study but cannot establish supervised procedural competence. OpenAnesthesia terms restrict reuse, including unauthorized commercial reuse.
practiceQuestions.domain: IV C regional anesthesia and patient safety

practiceQuestions.stem: A family has limited English proficiency. Which action best supports a safe preoperative conversation?

options.text: Use a child or family member as the default interpreter for complex consent.
Arrange an appropriate qualified interpreter, address the child/family directly, and verify understanding through a respectful process.
Skip questions that require nuanced explanation.
Assume a signed form proves understanding.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Communication and informed consent are integral professional and systems competencies. The OA resource specifically covers caring for families with limited English proficiency; local institutional interpretation policies apply.
practiceQuestions.domain: V professionalism, consent, communication and disparities

practiceQuestions.stem: An educational video presents a child with obesity. Which is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Obesity alone determines airway outcome and recovery location.
It is one part of individualized assessment; evaluate associated conditions, airway, procedure and recovery resources without assuming a diagnosis.
The video substitutes for current guidance.
Every child with obesity must receive the same anesthetic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A comorbidity label is not a complete risk assessment. The board outline lists obesity and related comorbidity among pre-op considerations; decisions must be individualized and source-current.
practiceQuestions.domain: IV A evaluation; II respiratory and cardiovascular

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional near miss occurs after confusing look-alike medication packaging. What is the most useful learning response?

options.text: Focus only on blaming the last person who handled the medication.
Prioritize immediate patient safety, follow institutional disclosure/reporting pathways, and analyze system contributors using a learning-focused process.
Avoid reporting if no injury occurred.
Publish the patient record in a teaching forum to warn others.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA special-problems topics include medication-error prevention, disclosure, human factors and QI; ACGME includes patient-safety educational activity. Protect privacy and use institutional procedures.

practiceQuestions.stem: An independent course has 36 target video hours in its catalog, but verified public video entries total less than that. What should the course report?

options.text: The target as completed hours.
Actual deduplicated runtime and exact gap; proposed original clips remain planned until produced, duration-probed and made accessible.
Estimated times for readings as videos.
Duplicate the same playlist to meet the target.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A target is not delivered media. Only publicly accessible unique recordings with observed durations are counted; plans, duplicated media, readings and unknown runtimes remain outside verified hours.
practiceQuestions.domain: V evidence-based practice and course media audit

assignment.instructions: For a fictional case supplied by instructor, produce a 1,200–1,500 word memo: state known anatomy/interventions, distinguish observed facts from assumptions, explain likely physiology and uncertainty, list missing records/questions, identify procedure/environment risks and needed consultants/resources, and describe a communication/postoperative handoff plan. Do not provide drug doses, a patient-specific order set, or procedure instructions. Present a 7-minute oral defense and respond to challenge questions.

rubric.excellent: Accurately describes circulation, relevant hemodynamic modifiers and uncertainty; avoids diagnosis-label anchoring.
Integrates current studies, comorbidities, procedure, prior interventions and resources; flags missing data.
Appropriate consultation/resource/destination considerations, closed-loop communication and contingencies, without unsupervised treatment directions.
Uses current authoritative sources, distinguishes evidence from inference, protects privacy and communicates clearly.

assignment.passingGuidance: Educator-set formative threshold only; not a validated assessment and not evidence of clinical competency.

assessment.format: Formative, source-cited assessments: 10 original single-best-answer items in this file; unit concept maps; fictional case reasoning; one final memo/oral defense.
assessment.standard: Suggested educational scoring only; no validated pass prediction, credential, board representation, or clinical competency rating.

studyHours.description: Suggested self-study plan: approximately 36 hours actual video target (not met), 48 hours primary readings/notes, 24 hours case reasoning/retrieval practice, 12 hours capstone and review. unitMap.text: Foundations: anatomy, segmental description, fetal transition and circulation
coveredTopics: Cardiac anatomy and nomenclature; transitional circulation; pressure-flow-resistance; oxygen content versus saturation; shunt reasoning.

unitMap.text: Preoperative assessment, risk stratification and preparation
coveredTopics: Records and imaging review; baseline saturation/hematology; airway; fasting/medication context; risk communication; escalation/resources.

unitMap.text: Anesthesia pharmacology and hemodynamic goals by lesion physiology
coveredTopics: Induction/maintenance choices; myocardial depression; pulmonary vasoreactivity; ventilation effects; vasoactive support principles.

unitMap.text: Lesion-based clinical reasoning: shunts and obstructive lesions
coveredTopics: Left-to-right shunt, cyanosis, ductal dependence as relevant, RV outflow obstruction, coarctation, repaired lesions and residual disease.

unitMap.text: Single-ventricle pathway and staged palliation
coveredTopics: HLHS and other single-ventricle variants; shunt-dependent pulmonary flow; Glenn/Fontan physiology; late sequelae.

unitMap.text: Cardiopulmonary bypass, myocardial protection, temperature and coagulation
coveredTopics: Circuit/prime concepts; bypass and separation; hypothermia/DHCA/SCP terminology; blood management; coagulation and transfusion decisions.

unitMap.text: Monitoring, echocardiography and imaging integration
coveredTopics: Invasive pressure/flow monitoring; NIRS; TEE fundamentals; cath hemodynamics; MRI/CT environment and remote-site risk.

unitMap.text: Catheterization, electrophysiology and non-operating-room anesthesia
coveredTopics: Diagnostic vs intervention; ablation/pacing; device considerations; sedation/general anesthesia contexts; rescue capability.

unitMap.text: Pulmonary hypertension, ventricular dysfunction and acute instability
coveredTopics: PVR triggers; RV/LV failure; pulmonary hypertensive crisis; arrhythmia; tamponade; residual lesion; low cardiac output.

unitMap.text: Noncardiac procedures in congenital heart disease
coveredTopics: Anatomy/physiology review; syndromic/airway/organ sequelae; postoperative respiratory/cardiovascular complications; systems.

unitMap.text: Postoperative cardiac critical care, mechanical support and transitions
coveredTopics: Cardiac ICU handover; low cardiac output; bleeding; ventilation; ECMO/circulatory support; transplant; team communication.

unitMap.text: Safety, professionalism, QI, evidence appraisal and lifelong learning
coveredTopics: Milestone competencies; quality metrics; human factors; fatigue/communication; statistics; research ethics; knowledge limits.

topicGaps: Observed free recording ledger: 12156 seconds (3.376667 h) from five eligible unique recordings; target is 36 h; remaining gap is 32.623333 h. Original scripts and targetMinutes are not videos and do not count.

Recordings offer partial foundations on CHD classification, fetal transition, lesions, noncardiac CHD risk, imaging and cath concepts; they do not constitute a complete pediatric cardiac anesthesia curriculum.

No verified accessible full-length specialist recording was found for pediatric CPB/anesthetic management and myocardial protection, deep hypothermia/circulatory arrest or selective cerebral perfusion, pediatric coagulation/transfusion, TEE practice/scope, EP procedural management, comprehensive pulmonary-hypertensive crisis reasoning, postoperative ECMO/VAD/ICU transitions, or safety/QI/professionalism. These domains require source-grounded production and supervised clinical training.

CCAS lecture materials and webinars are member-login restricted; not accessed. CHOP OPEN pages describe a free Heart Talks series but require free-account registration/login to enroll; playback duration/access were not independently verified and none were counted.

Only about 9.38% of the 36-hour floor is supported by verified eligible recordings. The 32.623333-hour residual remains unmet; further relevant recordings may exist, but were not verified in this research run.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn is described only as having a “cyanotic lesion.” Which next step best supports physiologic planning?

options.text: Assume low pulmonary blood flow and avoid all reductions in SVR
Clarify sequential segmental anatomy, current connections/palliation, mixing, ventricular function, and current hemodynamics
Use diagnosis label alone to select a fixed anesthetic
Treat baseline saturation as proof of adequate systemic oxygen delivery

practiceQuestions.rationale: A label does not define current circulation. Segmental anatomy, prior intervention, physiology and context are needed; saturation alone is not oxygen content or perfusion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with repaired CHD is scheduled for a noncardiac procedure. Which assessment is most appropriate?

options.text: Risk depends only on whether the original lesion was cyanotic
Review current physiology, residual lesions, ventricular function, rhythm, pulmonary vascular status, comorbidities, procedure and available resources
All repaired CHD can be managed as routine without record review
The most recent problem-list diagnosis is sufficient

practiceQuestions.rationale: Current residual physiology, sequelae and procedural/resource context inform risk; “repaired” does not establish normal physiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which principle is most defensible when considering a lesion with a left-to-right shunt?

options.text: Shunt magnitude is fixed regardless of SVR/PVR or clinical state
Flow is influenced by pressure/resistance relationships and anatomy; reassess the individual physiology
A high oxygen saturation excludes important cardiovascular disease
A single induction technique is universally optimal

practiceQuestions.rationale: Shunt flow depends on anatomy and changing hemodynamic conditions. Avoid universal recipes and reassess case-specific physiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a patient with a Fontan circulation, which conceptual point is important?

options.text: Pulmonary blood flow is driven by a subpulmonary ventricle
Pulmonary blood flow depends substantially on the transpulmonary pathway and low-resistance pulmonary circulation; ventricular function and venous pressure matter
Systemic arterial saturation alone defines adequate output
Prior Fontan completion removes need to assess rhythm and ventricular function

practiceQuestions.rationale: Fontan physiology lacks a subpulmonary pumping chamber; venous pressure, pulmonary vascular resistance, ventricular function, rhythm and anatomy all matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A perioperative team is reviewing a complex CHD patient for a remote-site MRI. Which systems question is most relevant?

options.text: Whether the MRI room is quiet
Whether monitoring, airway access, rescue equipment, staffing, communication and recovery resources match the anticipated risk
Whether the patient has had any previous anesthetic
Whether imaging itself guarantees low risk

practiceQuestions.rationale: Remote-site safety requires a coordinated plan for monitoring/access/rescue and recovery; imaging location does not eliminate anesthetic risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a case, oxygenation and perfusion change abruptly. What is the best cognitive approach?

options.text: Attribute the change immediately to the known lesion
Use a structured differential including airway/ventilation, circuit, hemodynamics, rhythm, surgical/cannula factors and evolving physiology, and call for appropriate help
Increase one vasoactive drug without reassessment
Wait for the next scheduled blood test

practiceQuestions.rationale: A known lesion does not explain every event. Systematic differential diagnosis, rapid reassessment and team escalation are safer than anchoring.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about board certification is accurate based on ABA public exam information?

options.text: ABA lists a separate pediatric cardiac anesthesiology certification exam
ABA lists pediatric anesthesiology certification, but the cited public exam page does not list a distinct pediatric cardiac anesthesiology board exam
Completing any cardiac rotation confers board eligibility
A course certificate guarantees exam eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABA page describes pediatric anesthesiology certification; no distinct pediatric cardiac exam is listed there. Eligibility is board-defined and is not conferred by this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellow sees an apparent ACGME case-minimum requirement in the current program requirements. What may an independent learner conclude?

options.text: They have met that requirement by reading a lecture
They may use it as a description of accredited clinical training standards, but case experience/competence requires supervised patient care and program verification
A simulation can automatically replace every required patient case
The curriculum confers eligibility once the outline is completed

practiceQuestions.rationale: Requirements describe accredited training experiences, not educational self-study substitutes. Course completion cannot attest clinical case volume or competency.

practiceQuestions.stem: A team plans to use a CCAS slide deck linked from its lecture page. What access limitation is stated by CCAS?

options.text: All materials carry an unrestricted CC BY license
The lecture documents require CCAS member login
The documents are public domain
Any file link means reuse and redistribution are allowed

practiceQuestions.rationale: CCAS explicitly says member login is required for the lecture documents; access and reuse rights should not be assumed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which use of an open-access case image is appropriate for this course?

options.text: Download and place it in course materials because viewing is free
Link to the original source and check its specific license and terms before reuse; do not copy identifiable patient records or images
Remove a watermark and redistribute
Use it as proof of local clinical outcome

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free viewing is not a reuse license. Link rather than rehost, verify image-specific terms, and respect de-identification/privacy.

topicGaps: Verified free recording coverage remains 34.1714 hours below the 36-hour video target. Only 1.8286 unique observed hours are counted; authored scripts and planned production targets are not recordings.

No counted recordings yet cover current 2026 pediatric sepsis guideline teaching, detailed PARDS definition/recommendations, pediatric cardiac arrest current guidance, renal replacement/CRRT, ECMO/ECLS, sedation/delirium, trauma/toxicology, ethical/end-of-life care, QI, or research methods.

The two newly counted recordings are older OPENPediatrics mechanical-ventilation teaching resources (2016); use as conceptual supplements, not current guideline content or independent practice instruction.

Promising shock, cardiopulmonary, noninvasive ventilation, ARDS, ECMO, post-arrest neurocritical, TBI, and sepsis videos were excluded when direct public playback, unique ID, exact runtime, or no-login access could not be verified. See unknownDurationItems for observed access gaps.

The OPENPediatrics Critical Content playlist (65 entries) and Stanford Digital Medic six-video playlist remain uncounted because the prior packet has no item-level runtime ledger; no duration is inferred.

Current source-backed instruction remains insufficient for several ABP domains, especially procedures, renal/electrolyte, infection/immunology, hematology/oncology, endocrine/metabolic, GI/nutrition, trauma/toxicology, sedation/analgesia, end-of-life, ethics, leadership, QI, and scholarly activity.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the 2026 SSC guideline recommend measuring in the initial evaluation of probable sepsis or suspected septic shock?

options.text: Blood lactate
Routine procalcitonin for every antibiotic decision
Routine pulmonary-artery catheterization
One universal blood-pressure percentile

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current guideline recommends lactate in initial evaluation; it does not recommend routine procalcitonin for de-escalation when stewardship programs are effective and has no universal BP-percentile target.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes antibiotic timing for suspected septic shock from probable sepsis without shock in the 2026 SSC guideline?

options.text: Both require antibiotics within 15 minutes.
Shock: start as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour; without shock: rapid time-limited investigation, then if concern is substantiated start as soon as possible, ideally within 3 hours.
Wait for final cultures and susceptibilities.
Avoid empiric therapy in shock.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The recommendations distinguish suspected shock and probable sepsis without shock; obtain cultures first only when doing so does not substantially delay therapy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teaching question asks what must accompany fluid boluses in pediatric septic shock. What is the 2026 SSC answer?

options.text: Continue to a fixed volume regardless of examination.
Reassess after each bolus, titrate to clinical markers and stop boluses if shock resolves or fluid overload develops.
Use albumin as mandatory first-line fluid.
Do not reassess until one hour later.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline's good-practice statement requires reassessment after every bolus and discontinuation if shock resolves or overload appears; crystalloid is suggested over albumin for initial resuscitation.

practiceQuestions.stem: After resuscitation for pediatric sepsis, what oxygenation target strategy does the 2026 SSC guideline conditionally suggest?

options.text: A conservative SpO₂ range of 88–92% rather than a more liberal target above 94%.
100% saturation in every child.
No oxygen even with hypoxemia.
Ignore baseline and context in cyanotic heart disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current guideline conditionally suggests titrating supplemental oxygen to a conservative 88–92% range after resuscitation rather than a liberal >94% target; context still matters.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best summarizes the PALICC-2 PARDS definition framework?

options.text: Hypoxemia alone is sufficient.

It considers timing within 7 days, new opacities not primarily due to atelectasis/effusion, edema not fully explained by cardiac failure/fluid overload, and oxygenation criteria; severity stratification is at least 4 hours after diagnosis.
Airway obstruction alone is PARDS.
A normal initial image permanently excludes PARDS.

practiceQuestions.rationale: PALICC-2 uses a multidimensional definition and delayed severity stratification; isolated airway-obstructive respiratory failure is not classified as possible/at-risk PARDS.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is consistent with the 2025 AHA/AAP PALS guidance for initial pediatric arrest rhythm?

options.text: Epinephrine before defibrillation for every shockable rhythm.
Give epinephrine as soon as possible for initial nonshockable rhythm; rapid defibrillation remains the priority for initial shockable rhythm.
Delay CPR until access is established.
Give bicarbonate and calcium routinely in every arrest.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 guideline emphasizes early epinephrine for initial nonshockable rhythms and rapid defibrillation for shockable rhythms; bicarbonate/calcium are not routine except special circumstances.

practiceQuestions.stem: How should the Pediatric Severe TBI guideline's suggested CPP range be described?

options.text: A strong Level I requirement for exactly 50 mm Hg at every age.
Weak Level III suggestions include minimum 40 mm Hg and a 40–50 mm Hg range, with possible age-specific thresholds.
CPP should never be considered.
A normal early CT excludes raised ICP.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Brain Trauma Foundation labels these weak Level III suggestions and notes possible age differences; normal initial CT does not exclude raised ICP in a comatose child.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the 2026 SSC guideline say about VV-ECMO for children with sepsis?

options.text: Routine first-line therapy for any hypoxemia.
It conditionally suggests VV-ECMO for refractory hypoxia despite other therapies; this does not establish an individual candidacy decision or procedural competence.
A substitute for multidisciplinary review.
VA-ECMO for every child with sepsis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The recommendation is conditional and based on very-low-certainty evidence; selection/support requires specialist, center-specific multidisciplinary evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which non-acute-care topic set appears in the ABP PCCM content outline?

options.text: End of life, PICU coordination, leadership/professionalism, clinical ethics and scholarly activity.
Only ventilation and procedures.
Only outpatient well-child care.
No QI or research.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ten ABP domains include end of life, PICU management, professionalism/leadership/advocacy/education, clinical ethics, and scholarly activity.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about independent study and ABP certification eligibility is accurate?

options.text: Course completion substitutes for fellowship and grants eligibility.
ABP requires qualifying accredited training, scholarly activity/program verification and a passing subspecialty exam; this course confers none of these.
There is no separate ABP PCCM exam.
An online course guarantees passing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP states three years of full-time accredited fellowship, scholarly activity, verification and passing the subspecialty examination are required. Self-study confers no eligibility or certification.

topicGaps: The duration-verified free public-recording ledger is 9.8056 hours against the 36-hour target; 26.1944 hours remain. Scripts and production targets are not recorded video and do not reduce this gap.

The public recording inventory is uneven: atopic dermatitis, neonatal topics, genodermatoses, vascular anomalies, broad update, social context and melanoma have some viewing coverage, but this does not constitute complete instruction in any unit.

Substantial recording/source gaps remain for papulosquamous and medication reactions; genodermatoses/cornification; infections and infestations; blistering/immunobullous disease; acne, hair and nail differentials; pediatric tumors and photosensitivity; systemic/oncology/rheumatology consultation; dermatopathology, procedures, QI and scholarship.

No full public BCH institutional didactic series, weighted public ABD exam blueprint, or separate foundation-hour ledger was identified. The publicly accessible course remains a partial curriculum, not a clinical-training substitute.
One existing record, L8, remains without verified duration/access and excluded. Video public-watch availability is not equivalent to tested playback or reuse/embedding permission.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (independent educational self-study; not a fellowship programme)
boardNames: American Board of Dermatology (ABD): Pediatric Dermatology subspecialty certification examination (requires primary ABD dermatology certification)
American Osteopathic Board of Dermatology (AOBD): separate osteopathic pediatric dermatology subspecialty certification pathway; not interchangeable with ABD certification
medical.boardStatus: Actual physician subspecialty: yes. ABD explicitly offers Pediatric Dermatology subspecialty certification and exam, dependent on primary ABD dermatology certification, an ACGME-accredited pediatric dermatology fellowship, unrestricted license and other current rules. AOBD separately advertises a DO subspecialty route; Boston Children’s says its fellowship accepts candidates eligible for ABD and Massachusetts licensure. This is not a generic directory-only label, combined programme, research-only appointment or non-physician supplement. No evidence of a Johns Hopkins variant was identified for this named track; the assigned institutional variant is Boston Children’s only.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course confers no ABD/AOBD board eligibility, exam credit, certification, licensure or accredited training. ABD requires primary ABD dermatology certification and additional ACGME-accredited pediatric dermatology fellowship training; current official criteria control. BCH states fellows must be eligible for ABD and Massachusetts medical licensure. AOBD is a distinct certifier/pathway. Verify with each board.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School teaching hospital)
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Dermatology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page lists two ACGME-accredited positions, ABD and Massachusetts licensure eligibility, 8 half-days/week clinic/procedure settings, continuity clinic, vascular anomalies, dermatology-oncology/rheumatology, genodermatoses, atopic dermatitis, patch, acne/peeling and hair clinics, inpatient/newborn/ICU consults, journal club and grand rounds. Public page is a partial outline, not complete public didactics. Do not infer individual trainee case counts or supervised competence.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Dermatology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exactly the named BCH fellowship variant in the MED-154 packet. Harvard-affiliated institutional context is BCH; no separate Johns Hopkins pediatric dermatology variant established for this item. No combined programme. Research is part of fellowship scholarly activity, not a substitute specialty. Not non-physician.
sourceCaveats: Official BCH, ABD and ACGME public pages consulted; the ACGME Pediatric Dermatology requirements linked for effect July 1, 2026. Public institutional descriptions are not complete curricular hour logs.

The ABD Pediatric Dermatology webpage describes one or more additional fellowship years; do not infer eligibility solely from course completion. BCH lists ACGME-accredited positions and requires ABD eligibility and MA licensure, without publicly exposing a full didactic syllabus.

A separate ABD subspecialty exam exists (ABD says approximately 4h/200 MCQs); AOBD advertises a distinct osteopathic route. No official weighted public pediatric subspecialty exam blueprint was found in accessible sources; curriculum domains are mapped qualitatively to ABD fellowship core curriculum, not fabricated percentages.

YouTube video durations came from stateless yt-dlp public YouTube search-result metadata, not from downloading media. Direct watch playback was not smoke-tested; free access status therefore means public listing/no paywall flag, not a guarantee of future playback. Unknown durations and access status are excluded from hours.

Video publication dates shown by search metadata are approximate/platform result dates; year-only/unknown dates retained as null. Do not interpret PeDRA/third-party recordings as BCH/Harvard teaching.

Clinical guidance changes; notably AAD pediatric AD recommendations are updated and product age indications require checking current labels. AAP IH guideline is 2019 and must be checked against current specialist guidance.
No patient records or diagnostic image files copied. Linked educational images have not undergone independent consent/provenance audit. Human clinical review not performed.

topicGaps: The duration-verified free public-recording ledger is 9.8056 hours against the 36-hour target; 26.1944 hours remain. Scripts and production targets are not recorded video and do not reduce this gap.

The public recording inventory is uneven: atopic dermatitis, neonatal topics, genodermatoses, vascular anomalies, broad update, social context and melanoma have some viewing coverage, but this does not constitute complete instruction in any unit.

Substantial recording/source gaps remain for papulosquamous and medication reactions; genodermatoses/cornification; infections and infestations; blistering/immunobullous disease; acne, hair and nail differentials; pediatric tumors and photosensitivity; systemic/oncology/rheumatology consultation; dermatopathology, procedures, QI and scholarship.

No full public BCH institutional didactic series, weighted public ABD exam blueprint, or separate foundation-hour ledger was identified. The publicly accessible course remains a partial curriculum, not a clinical-training substitute.
One existing record, L8, remains without verified duration/access and excluded. Video public-watch availability is not equivalent to tested playback or reuse/embedding permission.
