practiceQuestions.stem: A 2-month-old has a newly enlarging periocular vascular-appearing lesion. Which learning priority best follows AAP guidance?

options.text: Diagnose a hemangioma from location alone
Prompt specialist assessment because of possible functional risk and growth window
Reassure because most infantile hemangiomas resolve
Begin systemic medicine from this vignette

practiceQuestions.rationale: Periocular lesions may threaten function; potentially problematic IHs merit early evaluation/referral. A text vignette does not establish diagnosis or authorize treatment. [S4]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best characterizes the growth timeline summarized in the AAP infantile hemangioma guideline?

options.text: Most rapid growth is after age 2 years
Most rapid growth occurs 1–3 months; growth is complete by 5 months in most cases
All growth ends at birth
Growth timing is identical for all vascular malformations

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP describes fastest/significant IH growth between 1 and 3 months, completed by 5 months in most; this is not a rule for every vascular anomaly. [S4]

practiceQuestions.stem: A red lesion is fully formed at birth. What is the safest classification approach?

options.text: Call every vascular lesion infantile hemangioma
Consider congenital hemangioma and malformation categories; classify using clinical context and specialist assessment
Assume it will involute like an IH
Use the term port-wine stain for all lesions

practiceQuestions.rationale: Lesion timing informs differential; congenital hemangioma and vascular malformation differ from infantile hemangioma. The ISSVA framework supports precise terminology. [S12]

practiceQuestions.stem: A few classic honey-crusted lesions are present on a child; no systemic concerns are described. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Physical exam can never diagnose impetigo
Nonbullous impetigo can involve S. pyogenes, S. aureus, or both; routine testing is not always required
All cases require blood cultures
Streptococcal vs staphylococcal cause is reliably distinguished by appearance

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC says nonbullous impetigo may be caused by GAS, S. aureus, or both; exam diagnosis is typical and exam alone cannot reliably differentiate bacterial cause. [S6]

practiceQuestions.stem: A child’s presumed atopic dermatitis is not responding despite a carefully reviewed plan. What is an evidence-aligned next reasoning step?

options.text: Escalate automatically to systemic steroids
Reassess diagnosis, adherence/exposure and mimics; consult current pediatric guideline and specialist where appropriate
Assume allergy testing is mandatory in all children
Stop all skin care

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guidance emphasizes evidence-based pediatric management; persistent apparent treatment failure should prompt diagnostic reassessment rather than reflexive escalation. Check current recommendations and individual circumstances. [S5] [S10]

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the main reason the AAD pediatric atopic dermatitis page must be date-checked?

options.text: Its recommendations never change
Therapies, approvals, age labels and evidence can evolve; the page carries current and updated recommendations
Only adult care is addressed
Guidelines eliminate clinical judgment

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAD maintains and updates its guidance; pediatric therapy labels and available agents can change. Confirm current recommendations/label and patient-specific factors. [S5]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which resource offers pediatric modules on newborn rashes, genetic skin disease, pediatric fungal disease and vascular lesions?

options.text: Only ACGME case logs
SPD/AAD Basic Dermatology Curriculum modules
ABD examination questions
A commercial image bank

practiceQuestions.rationale: SPD links pediatric-specific modules hosted within AAD Basic Dermatology Curriculum. Module access terms may vary. [S7]

practiceQuestions.stem: An infant has blistering and mucosal involvement. Which approach best represents safe consult reasoning?

options.text: Use one image to name an inherited blistering disorder definitively
Treat as an urgent assessment problem, describe morphology/systemic status and involve appropriate specialist team
Defer review until routine follow-up
Use this course to authorize biopsy independently

practiceQuestions.rationale: Blistering plus mucosal/systemic signs can signal serious disease; clinical assessment and expert-directed testing are needed. ABD curriculum expects supervised diagnostic and consult skills; this course grants no procedural competence. [S2]

practiceQuestions.stem: What does completing this independent course confer?

options.text: ABD pediatric dermatology certificate
ACGME fellowship credit and board eligibility
Self-study only; no institutional affiliation, accreditation, licensure, eligibility or certification
Authority to perform lasers under sedation

practiceQuestions.rationale: Board certification requires formal prerequisites and fellowship/examination under ABD; this course is independent and does not replace supervised accredited clinical training. [S2] [S3]

practiceQuestions.stem: The public ABD page states pediatric dermatology certification is contingent on what primary board status?

options.text: Primary certification by ABD in dermatology
Board certification in pediatrics only
No primary certification
Completion of an online course

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABD states primary ABD dermatology certification is prerequisite to its pediatric dermatology subspecialty certification; separate routes/boards must not be conflated. [S2]

title: Pediatric Emergency Medicine Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced medical learner with prior medical sciences and pediatric foundations; this is not an entry-level lay course.
Recommended prior coursework: pediatric assessment, basic physiology, evidence appraisal, and emergency stabilization principles.
Self-study assumes familiarity with clinical terminology. Actual patient care requires credentialed supervision, current local protocols and applicable licensure.
objectives: Reason through pediatric emergencies using age-specific physiology, acuity, differential diagnosis, diagnostic selection, response to therapy and disposition.
Map learning to the ABP PEM exam outline applicable on the examination date, while recognizing the outline is not a full curriculum.
Assess pathway/guideline eligibility, exclusions, evidence currency and individual applicability.
Explain systems, EMS, trauma, toxicology, environmental, safeguarding, behavioral, procedural and scholarly foundations of PEM.
Communicate uncertainty, safe transitions, family-centered care and limits of self-study.
Distinguish theoretical knowledge from supervised clinical and procedural competence.

units.title: Emergency-department assessment, acuity, diagnostic reasoning and disposition
objectives: Apply age-specific physiology and an organized initial assessment to identify immediate threats.
Construct ranked differentials and select tests using pretest probability, decision rules and potential harms.
Reassess response to interventions and justify consultation, observation, transfer or discharge with safety-netting.
topics: Universal tasks: core science, diagnosis and patient management
Triage, history/exam, risk stratification, diagnostic stewardship, shared decisions, disposition and return precautions
boardDomains: Current D1 Emergency Conditions; D2 Resuscitation; D27 ED Operations/Patient Rights
2027 D3–24 condition-specific domains; D27 ED Operations/Patient Rights
casePractice: Choose a Nationwide Children’s pathway and identify inclusion criteria, exclusions and escalation triggers; do not treat the pathway as a universal order.

assessment.rubric: 10 points: acuity/dangerous alternative (3), relevant data and limitations (2), proportionate testing (2), reassessment/disposition (2), safety-net communication (1).

units.title: Common acute medical conditions across infancy, childhood and adolescence
objectives: Differentiate common from time-critical respiratory, infectious, neurologic, cardiac, abdominal, metabolic and allergic presentations.
Use age, appearance, trajectory and comorbidity to recognize when a focused pathway does not apply.
Integrate guideline evidence with individual context and communicate diagnostic uncertainty.
topics: Respiratory distress/wheeze/croup/bronchiolitis
Fever/infection, seizures/headache, vomiting/dehydration, endocrine/metabolic, allergic and cardiac emergencies
casePractice: Use text cases and pathways to compare bronchiolitis, asthma, fever and seizure differentials. Cases are learning prompts, not care orders.

assessment.rubric: 20 points: age/context (4), differential/risk (5), evidence applicability (4), management priorities without unsupported dosing (4), reassessment/follow-up (3).

units.title: Neonatal and young-infant emergencies
objectives: Distinguish the AAP febrile-infant guideline population from infants it expressly excludes.
Explain why ill appearance, prematurity, comorbidity or other exclusions require a different evidence-based pathway.
Analyze age-specific infection risk and uncertainty without applying a decision algorithm outside its scope.
topics: Well-appearing febrile infants 8–60 days; documented fever, gestational-age limits, excluded groups; neonatal instability, hypothermia, sepsis/HSV differential
boardDomains: Current D1 Emergency Conditions; D2 Resuscitation; D8 Special Populations
2027 D2 Resuscitation; D3 Infectious; D5 Special Populations; D6 Neonatal Conditions
casePractice: Complete AAP guideline applicability checklist for fictional 21-day, 34-week corrected and ill-appearing infant scenarios; name why guideline cannot be applied in excluded scenarios.

assessment.rubric: 15 points: eligibility criterion accuracy (6), exclusion recognition (5), risk/differential and escalation (2), uncertainty and source citation (2).

units.title: Pediatric resuscitation, shock and respiratory failure
objectives: Recognize compensated deterioration and organize team communication using a structured approach.
Interpret age-specific physiology and prioritize airway, breathing, circulation, glucose and reversible causes.
Use simulation debriefing to identify cognitive, teamwork and system factors; do not infer procedural competence.
topics: Initial resuscitation, shock, respiratory failure, cardiac arrest, arrhythmia, seizure stabilization, handoff and post-event debrief
boardDomains: 2027 D1 Trauma; D2 Resuscitation; D4 Procedures
casePractice: EM Sim Cases: pediatric drowning, asthma, status epilepticus and SVT; use fictional scenarios and debrief only; no patient images.

assessment.rubric: 20 points: early recognition (4), prioritized actions (5), team roles/closed-loop communication (4), reassessment/escalation (4), reflective debrief (3).

units.title: Pediatric trauma, head injury and musculoskeletal injury
objectives: Assess mechanism and physiology while maintaining an age-appropriate trauma differential.
Use validated decision tools within inclusion criteria and balance missed injury against imaging harms.
Apply current pediatric mild-TBI recommendations to symptoms, return-to-activity counseling and follow-up.
topics: Primary/secondary survey, head/spine/chest/abdominal injury, fractures, drowning/thermal injury, concussion and decision rules
boardDomains: Current D3 Trauma; D1 Emergency Conditions
2027 D1 Trauma; D4 Procedures; D24 Musculoskeletal/Orthopedic; D15 Environmental Emergencies
casePractice: EM Sim Cases pediatric trauma and drowning; CDC mild TBI checklist. Do not copy diagnostic images; use links only.

assessment.rubric: 15 points: risk stratification (4), tool applicability (3), imaging rationale (3), symptom-based discharge/follow-up (3), source citation (2).

units.title: Toxicology and environmental emergencies
objectives: Build a structured exposure history and assess toxidrome, physiology, time course and co-ingestants.
Differentiate high-risk ingestion, medication error and environmental exposure while using poison-center/consultation escalation appropriately.
Compare hazards such as heat/cold, drowning, bites/stings and carbon monoxide without relying on stale dose charts.
topics: Acetaminophen and other ingestions, toxidromes, decontamination concepts, poison-center consultation, hypothermia/heat illness, drowning
boardDomains: Current D4 Toxicology; D5 Environmental Emergencies; D2 Resuscitation
2027 D7 Toxicology; D15 Environmental Emergencies; D2 Resuscitation
casePractice: Review the linked institutional ingestion pathways and EM Sim Cases drowning case; identify local poison center as current escalation resource.

assessment.rubric: 15 points: exposure/symptom timeline (4), physiologic risk (4), evidence source/currency (3), escalation and reassessment (2), no unsupported dosing (2).

units.title: Child maltreatment, safeguarding and mandatory systems response
objectives: Recognize when history, developmental capability, injury pattern or clinical course raises safeguarding concerns.
Document observations objectively and distinguish clinical findings from attribution or legal conclusions.
Plan consultation, safety, mandated reporting and trauma-informed communication in accordance with jurisdictional law.
topics: Physical abuse/maltreatment, neglect, sexual abuse/trafficking, differential diagnosis, forensic boundaries, reporting, bias and safe disposition
boardDomains: Current D6 Child Abuse and Maltreatment; D1 Emergency Conditions; D12 ED Operations
2027 D8 Child Abuse/Maltreatment; D27 ED Operations/Patient Rights
casePractice: Use Nationwide Children’s non-accidental trauma pathway as an example; follow local law and institutional child-protection experts. No real records or images copied.

assessment.rubric: 15 points: objective description (4), differential without premature conclusion (3), immediate safety (3), appropriate consultation/reporting (3), trauma-informed language/confidentiality (2).

units.title: Behavioral health, psychosocial emergencies and special populations
objectives: Conduct structured immediate safety assessment for agitation, self-harm risk or acute behavioral change while considering medical causes.
Adapt assessment and disposition for disability, medical complexity, communication needs, pregnancy/adolescence and social context.
Use family-centered, culturally responsive communication and identify constraints in local resources.
topics: Suicidality/self-harm, agitation, psychosis, substance exposure, exploitation, special health-care needs, pregnancy, communication barriers, social determinants
boardDomains: Current D7 Behavioral Health/Psychosocial; D8 Special Populations
2027 D5 Special Populations; D9 Behavioral/Psychosocial; D21 OB/Gyn
casePractice: Discuss a fictional agitation/self-harm case and map support, safety and consultation needs; no risk score is a substitute for clinical assessment.

assessment.rubric: 15 points: safety and medical differential (4), developmentally appropriate interview (3), inclusion/access considerations (3), consultation/disposition (3), respectful language (2).

units.title: Procedural knowledge, analgesia, sedation and point-of-care ultrasound
objectives: Explain indications, contraindications, preparation, consent/assent, monitoring and rescue planning for commonly used ED procedures.
Interpret point-of-care ultrasound within limits of training, image quality and pretest probability.
Distinguish cognitive knowledge and simulation from supervised competence, credentialing or authorization.
topics: Airway/procedural sedation concepts, vascular access, analgesia, wound care, reductions, POCUS applications, radiation stewardship and consent
casePractice: Read institutional descriptions of ultrasound teaching only as program-specific; no invasive or ultrasound skill is certified by this course.

assessment.rubric: 15 points: indication/alternatives (3), preprocedure risk and consent (3), monitoring/rescue/team (4), limitations (2), escalation/credentialing boundary (3).

units.title: EMS, transport, disaster readiness and mass-casualty response
objectives: Explain pediatric prehospital and interfacility handoff elements that affect stabilization and safe transitions.
Apply resource-aware planning to pediatric readiness, transport, disaster and mass-casualty scenarios.
Identify system roles, triage limits and continuity needs for children and caregivers.
topics: EMS and transport, medical control/handoff, disaster preparation, surge and reunification considerations, pediatric-specific equipment/readiness
boardDomains: Current D10 Disaster Preparedness; D11 EMS/Transport; D12 ED Operations
2027 D25 Mass Casualty/Disaster; D26 EMS/Transport; D27 ED Operations/Patient Rights
casePractice: National Pediatric Readiness Toolkit readiness gap review and fictional interfacility transfer handoff.

assessment.rubric: 15 points: identify safety risks (4), prioritize feasible changes (4), handoff/continuity plan (3), equity/family supports (2), measures and follow-up (2).

units.title: Emergency department operations, quality, ethics and patient rights
objectives: Describe pediatric ED readiness governance, interprofessional roles, quality measurement and continuous improvement.
Analyze flow, triage, communication, safety events and resource allocation using systems thinking.
Address assent/consent, confidentiality, access, bias and patient/family rights within applicable law and policy.
topics: Pediatric emergency care coordinators, equipment, policies, staff competency, QI, patient rights, transitions, boarding and resource stewardship
boardDomains: 2027 D27 ED Operations and Patient Rights
casePractice: Audit a publicly posted ED pathway against readiness and accessibility criteria; do not represent this exercise as an institutional audit.

assessment.rubric: 20 points: bounded problem (3), evidence and baseline measure (4), feasible change (4), equity/safety balancing measure (4), implementation/evaluation plan (3), rights/privacy (2).

units.title: Evidence appraisal, scholarship, integration and lifelong learning
objectives: Form a searchable clinical question, judge study design/bias and communicate uncertainty.
Integrate evidence into the 13-domain current blueprint and the 28-domain 2027 blueprint without treating either as a complete curriculum.
Construct a personal learning plan and recognize that exams do not measure all entrustable clinical activities.
topics: Clinical epidemiology, diagnostic accuracy, guideline appraisal, QI/research, ethics, knowledge translation, professional development and exam blueprint changes
boardDomains: Current D13 Core Knowledge in Scholarly Activities
2027 D28 Core Knowledge in Scholarly Activities; all content domains
casePractice: Compare the 2021 and 2027 blueprint domain structure and outline three clinical competencies that written tests cannot establish.

assessment.rubric: 20 points: focused question (3), source hierarchy/currency (4), bias/limitations (4), correct blueprint mapping (4), clinical applicability/uncertainty (3), no overclaiming (2).

assignment.title: Capstone: evidence-bounded pediatric ED learning case and readiness improvement proposal
assignment.instructions: Use an explicitly fictional educational vignette or a linked published case without copying content or images. Define age/context, immediate threats and differential; identify applicable guideline population and exclusions; map reasoning to current and April 2027 ABP blueprints; propose reassessment/disposition questions without issuing real-patient orders. Add a separate one-page systems improvement idea tied to the NPRP toolkit. Cite dated authoritative sources.

rubric.clinical reasoning and scope (25 points): Age/acuity, dangerous alternatives, inclusion/exclusion logic and uncertainty.
rubric.evidence appraisal and date checks (20 p: Primary-source use, currency, population fit, limitations.
rubric.safety and rights (10 points): Privacy, no patient-identifying material, no unsupported dosing or independent procedural claim.

assessment.formative: 10 original multiple-choice questions with rationales, unit worksheets, case debriefs and self-reflection.
assessment.summative: Capstone rubric score; recommended learner-selected threshold 80% for course completion only, not board readiness. Re-study missed domains and recheck source updates.
assessment.limits: Questions are original educational items, not official board content, validated predictor, or measure of clinical competence. No pass guarantee.

studyHours.plan: Approximately 120–160 self-study hours across readings, case discussion, assignments, question review and independent note preparation; planned study time is not recorded video time or clinical training time.
studyHours.note: No external video minutes verified; the planned clip series is not available media and does not reduce the gap.

It lists pediatric ED, pediatric critical care, anesthesia, trauma, toxicology, child abuse, EMS and adult EM experiences; curriculum page describes POCUS didactics, hands-on and simulation across all three years. This is the institution’s published track, not a claim that all PEM programs use the same length.

mapping.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School teaching hospital)
mapping.name: Pediatric Emergency Medicine | Fellowship Program
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official fellowship offering; publicly published curriculum shows a pediatrics-residency track over 3 years and an emergency-medicine-residency track over 2 years (with optional third year). Published rotations include ED, ultrasound, anesthesia, ICU, adult ED, toxicology, trauma, transport, EMS-related opportunities, research/QI and electives. This exact institutional schedule is preserved; does not establish a universally identical curriculum.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — Pediatric Emergency Medicine subspecialty certification
American Board of Emergency Medicine (ABEM) — credentialing/eligibility for EM-boarded PEM candidates

boardStatus.specialtyStatus: Pediatric Emergency Medicine is a clinical physician subspecialty/fellowship and has a separate PEM subspecialty certification examination. It is not a generic directory category, non-physician supplement, or research-only postdoctoral training item.
boardStatus.examStatus: There is one PEM certification examination developed and administered by ABP, with ABEM credentialing/eligibility processes for emergency-medicine-boarded candidates; no evidence of a second distinct ABEM PEM exam was found.
boardStatus.pathways: ACGME specifies separate prior-residency curricula: at least 36 months after pediatrics residency and at least 24 months after emergency-medicine residency. Institutional programs may exceed minimums. ABP and ABEM eligibility are not interchangeable; examinees must verify their own current board pathway.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course does not confer board eligibility. ABP eligibility page requires base certification in Pediatrics (ABP) or Emergency Medicine (ABEM), accredited PEM fellowship and additional published requirements for the ABP route. ABEM’s current PEM page describes its credentialing rules for EM-boarded candidates and references a separate dual-certification pathway. These are dated board rules and can change; verify directly with ABP/ABEM, including any AOBEM eligibility window (ABEM page notes a limited completion date through July 1, 2027).

officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official institutional page describes this as a three-year physician fellowship open to graduates of either pediatrics or emergency-medicine residency. This is the institution’s published track, not a claim that all PEM programs use the same length.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School teaching hospital)
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Emergency Medicine | Fellowship Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official fellowship offering; publicly published curriculum shows a pediatrics-residency track over 3 years and an emergency-medicine-residency track over 2 years (with optional third year). Published rotations include ED, ultrasound, anesthesia, ICU, adult ED, toxicology, trauma, transport, EMS-related opportunities, research/QI and electives. This exact institutional schedule is preserved; does not establish a universally identical curriculum.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact variant names/institutions retained from supplied packet. Johns Hopkins official page describes three years for either entry background; Boston Children’s publishes two-year EM and three-year pediatrics tracks. ACGME 2025 requirements set minimums of at least 24 months after EM residency and 36 months after pediatrics residency. These sources describe different things (institutional offering vs accreditation standard) and are not collapsed. Neither public program page exposes its complete internal lecture library or all proprietary cases. Harvard-affiliated institutional variant in this packet is Boston Children’s Hospital; no claim that these two programs exhaust all national PEM offerings.
sourceCaveats: No prior MED-155 curriculum or saved research files were present in the named paths, so this specialty set was constructed from scratch from the contract and packet.

unknownDurationItems.reason: Accessible duration not structurally supported by evidence.

topicGaps: Observed free public PEM video hours total 9.335556; 26.664444 hours remain to the 36-hour target. No original lecture is rendered, uploaded, or credited.

Recording coverage is selective rather than a lecture for each board topic. Unit 7 safeguarding, most of Units 5–9 and 11–12, detailed organ-system emergencies, behavioral emergencies, procedural competence, and scholarly methods remain without adequate verified recording coverage.
The 2025 livestream’s long runtime includes openings, transitions, audience questions, and pauses; runtime is not equivalent to uninterrupted didactic instruction or a quality/competence measure.
No foundation hours are separately counted; all counted recordings are PEM specialty teaching.

No current authoritative full free recorded course with a verified public runtime sufficient to close the residual gap was located. Additional high-quality source discovery and human specialty review are needed before treating coverage as complete.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A well-appearing, term 18-day-old infant is at home after newborn discharge and has a documented rectal temperature of 38.1°C. Which statement best describes use of the AAP 8–60-day guideline?

options.text: It is within the guideline age and population, subject to all eligibility checks and the age-specific algorithm.
It applies only after 28 days.
It applies only if the infant has respiratory symptoms.
It applies to any febrile neonate regardless of appearance or gestational age.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline covers well-appearing, term infants 8–60 days meeting its fever and setting criteria. Eligibility and exclusions still matter; do not generalize to ill-appearing infants or excluded populations.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 12-day-old infant is ill-appearing and febrile. What is the safest interpretation of the AAP well-appearing febrile-infant algorithm?

options.text: Apply its lowest-risk branch because age under 28 days is represented.
Do not apply it; ill-appearing infants are outside scope and require urgent evaluation using appropriate clinical pathways.
Use only a viral test to determine disposition.
Delay evaluation until the infant becomes well appearing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline expressly does not address moderately/severely ill-appearing infants; if uncertain about appearance, it should not be used. It is not a substitute for urgent individualized care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with mild traumatic brain injury has no finding that independently requires imaging after a validated risk assessment. Which principle aligns with current CDC pediatric mTBI guidance?

options.text: Routine neuroimaging is required to diagnose mTBI.
Do not routinely image solely to diagnose mTBI; use validated age-appropriate symptoms tools and clinical judgment.
Keep every child at strict rest until all symptoms have disappeared.
Use adult decision tools without age adjustment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC guidance advises against routine imaging to diagnose pediatric mTBI, recommends age-appropriate symptom scales and individualized return to activity after no more than 1–2 days of rest.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner views a linked pediatric resuscitation simulation and performs well on its written debrief. What conclusion is warranted?

options.text: The learner is competent to independently perform invasive procedures.
The learner has earned board eligibility.
The exercise can assess cognitive reasoning/teamwork but does not establish supervised procedural competence or credentialing.
The simulation substitutes for ACGME fellowship clinical exposure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Simulation can support deliberate learning but cannot certify competence or replace supervised clinical training, institutional authorization or board requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: An ED wants to improve ability to care for critically ill children. Which is most consistent with the 2026 multi-society pediatric readiness policy?

options.text: Focus only on purchasing an airway cart.
Use coordinated readiness work covering governance, staff competencies, policies, equipment, safety and quality improvement.
Rely solely on annual individual CME.
Limit pediatric readiness efforts to tertiary children’s hospitals.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The policy describes readiness as a systems foundation spanning coordination, competencies, equipment/supplies, policies, safety and continuous quality improvement, across ED types.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellowship applicant completed an emergency medicine residency. Which statement accurately reflects ACGME program-length requirements as published in the 2025 PEM requirements?

options.text: Every route must be exactly 36 months.
The minimum is 24 months for EM-residency graduates and 36 months for pediatrics-residency graduates; individual institutions may offer a longer program.
An EM residency graduate is not eligible for PEM fellowship.
The requirements are the same as board examination eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME specifies at least 24 months for EM graduates and 36 months for pediatric graduates. Institutional schedules may be longer; eligibility is separately governed by the boards.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which board-exam statement is accurate for PEM as of the reviewed ABEM page?

options.text: ABEM and ABP administer unrelated PEM exams.
There is no PEM subspecialty exam.
There is a PEM subspecialty certification examination developed/administered by ABP; ABEM credentialing/eligibility applies to emergency-medicine-boarded candidates.
The 2027 outline is the only content outline regardless of test date.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABEM’s page describes candidate eligibility/credentialing and says ABP develops and administers the PEM certification exam. Exam blueprint version depends on exam date.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has a witnessed new-onset seizure and returns toward baseline. Which source use is most appropriate for the linked 2019 case report?

options.text: Treat its old medication statements as current universal orders.
Use it as a published case for differential-diagnosis discussion, check current guidance independently, and do not reuse figures/text without rights.
Assume PMC inclusion places it in the public domain.
Use the case as proof of a population-level risk estimate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The report is an authentic published educational case, but its treatment statements are dated, PMC access does not imply open license, and a single case cannot establish population estimates.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which blueprint is applicable to an ABP PEM exam administered May 2027?

options.text: The 13-domain outline effective until March 31, 2027.
The new 28-domain outline effective April 1, 2027 and after.
The ABEM general EM outline only.
No published blueprint.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP states the updated 28-domain outline applies to all examinations on or after April 1, 2027; the prior 13-domain outline applies through March 31, 2027.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reviews an institutional ED pathway for pediatric bronchiolitis. Which statement best describes its role?

options.text: It is a universally binding national guideline.
It is a local evidence-informed aid; assess scope, currency and local context and do not apply rigidly to every patient.
It substitutes for clinician reassessment.
Its use certifies the learner’s clinical competence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Nationwide Children’s describes pathways as evidence-informed recommendations intended to complement clinical judgment, not to be applied rigidly in all cases.

assignment.title: Longitudinal pediatric endocrine case-conference portfolio
assignment.instructions: For three constructed cases (one growth/puberty; one dysglycemia or neonatal hypoglycemia; one calcium/adrenal/thyroid/DSD selection), submit concise de-identified reasoning maps with initial problem representation, differential, evidence for/against, age-specific interpretation, next information needed, safety escalation, family-centered communication and two current sources. Add a one-page evidence appraisal of an assigned guideline and identify date, scope and limitations.

rubric.standard: Prioritized and age/development-aware; distinguishes evidence from assumption; includes important alternatives.

unitMap.text: Endocrine physiology, assays, and clinical reasoning
coveredTopics: Endocrine physiology, assays, and clinical reasoning
Explain hormone synthesis, secretion, feedback, receptor action, age-dependent physiology, assay limitations, and preanalytic/analytic interference.

Assay interpretation as a chain: specimen timing and handling, binding proteins, cross-reactivity, heterophile antibodies, biotin exposure, platform differences, and repeat/alternate-method confirmation when results conflict with phenotype.
Distinguish measured hormone concentration from secretion, bioactivity, tissue action, and clinical state; use age-, pubertal-stage-, pregnancy/exposure-, and illness-appropriate reference context.

unitMap.text: Pediatric diabetes and acute dysglycemia
coveredTopics: Pediatric diabetes and acute dysglycemia

Differentiate T1D, T2D, monogenic and secondary diabetes; recognize DKA/HHS and cerebral-injury risk; reason through fluids/insulin principles from current protocols without treating this course as an order set.
Separate autoimmune type 1, youth-onset type 2, monogenic, neonatal, medication-associated, and secondary diabetes hypotheses; do not infer type from body size or one antibody.
Dysglycemia emergencies: acid-base/ketone context, cerebral injury vigilance, and protocol-based escalation; this packet provides no fluids/insulin order set.

unitMap.text: Longitudinal diabetes care and technology
coveredTopics: Longitudinal diabetes care and technology
Interpret glycemic metrics, insulin-delivery/CGM concepts, psychosocial and family/team systems, hypoglycemia prevention, transition, screening and evolving disease-modifying options.
Technology interpretation: time-in-range/CGM limitations, data completeness, device access, alarm burden, family roles, school plans, transition and psychosocial burden.

Presymptomatic type 1 diabetes screening/staging is a changing area; confirm antibodies, distinguish stage definitions from treatment thresholds, and link results to supervised counseling/follow-up rather than autonomous intervention.

unitMap.text: Normal growth, short stature, tall stature, and GH/IGF axis
coveredTopics: Normal growth, short stature, tall stature, and GH/IGF axis
Calculate/interpret growth velocity and percentiles; integrate parental target, maturation, chronic disease, nutrition, skeletal clues, IGF-axis data, bone age and test limitations.
Interpret trajectory with measurement quality, birth/family context, nutrition, chronic illness, pubertal timing, proportion, skeletal clues and psychosocial context before assigning GH-axis disease.
GH/IGF biomarkers and stimulation tests are assay- and context-dependent; no isolated value or bone age establishes diagnosis or treatment indication.

unitMap.text: Thyroid across infancy, childhood, and adolescence
coveredTopics: Thyroid across infancy, childhood, and adolescence
Interpret TSH/free hormone patterns by age; approach newborn screen follow-up, hypothyroidism, Graves/thyroiditis, nodules, cancer risk, and discordant assays.
Newborn-screen follow-up and congenital hypothyroidism are time-sensitive pathways; interpret screening thresholds and confirmatory testing using current jurisdictional algorithms.
Discordant TFTs: review medications, intercurrent illness, binding proteins, supplement exposures (including biotin) and assay interference before rare central or receptor diagnoses.
Thyroid nodule/cancer assessment in children requires pediatric expertise; the added general pediatric lecture augments but does not replace current ATA guidance or specialist evaluation.

unitMap.text: Pubertal development, disorders, and reproductive endocrinology
coveredTopics: Pubertal development, disorders, and reproductive endocrinology
Map hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal maturation; distinguish normal variation from precocious or delayed puberty, menstrual disorders, hypogonadism, fertility risk, and medication effects.

Adolescent cycle interpretation depends on gynecologic age and persistence; separate physiologic pubertal variation from hypogonadism, amenorrhea, hyperandrogenism, medication effect and systemic illness.
Precocious/delayed puberty reasoning requires tempo and longitudinal context, not a single physical sign or uncontextualized gonadotropin value.

unitMap.text: Adrenal cortex, CAH, adrenal insufficiency, and endocrine emergencies
coveredTopics: Adrenal cortex, CAH, adrenal insufficiency, and endocrine emergencies
Use steroid synthesis logic; recognize neonatal salt-wasting/emergency concern; distinguish CAH, adrenal insufficiency, androgen excess, Cushing and adrenal mass workup.
Steroid synthesis maps should support mechanism recognition across CAH and adrenal insufficiency while separating disease-specific pediatric emergency protocols from adult therapeutics.
Cushing syndrome, androgen excess, adrenal tumors and adrenal medulla disorders require differential-first evaluation and age-appropriate referral.

unitMap.text: Hypothalamus, pituitary, vasopressin, and water balance
coveredTopics: Hypothalamus, pituitary, vasopressin, and water balance
Localize pituitary deficits/excess; interpret pituitary development/tumor syndromes; organize polyuria/polydipsia and dysnatremia differential; identify urgent CNS red flags.
Localize pituitary disorders across anterior/posterior axes; evaluate combined deficits, developmental midline disease, tumors and treatment sequelae as supervised clinical problems.
Water-balance assessment integrates measured serum/urine context, intake/output, medication, renal function and CNS history; provocative testing and correction plans are not self-study instructions.

unitMap.text: Hypoglycemia and neonatal endocrine-metabolic evaluation
coveredTopics: Hypoglycemia and neonatal endocrine-metabolic evaluation
Distinguish transitional neonatal physiology from persistent hypoglycemia risk; use critical-sample logic and recognize that point-of-care values and timing need laboratory/clinical context.

Use the timing, symptoms, laboratory confirmation and metabolic state to distinguish common transitional low glucose from persistent hypoglycemia disorders; obtain critical samples only within safe supervised clinical care.
Critical-sample analytes are mechanistic evidence, not a stand-alone algorithm; fasting tests are specialist-supervised and potentially hazardous.

unitMap.text: Differences of sex development, gonadal development, and gender medicine
coveredTopics: Differences of sex development, gonadal development, and gender medicine
Describe developmental pathways; organize a respectful, multidisciplinary initial evaluation; protect confidentiality, assent, family communication, and avoid rushed or deterministic decisions.
DSD work requires respectful, confidential multidisciplinary communication; distinguish chromosome/gonadal/hormonal/anatomic observations without forcing a premature label.
Gender-related care and policy are evolving and jurisdiction-dependent; source dates, current laws, assent/consent, psychosocial expertise and individual care-team guidance are essential.

unitMap.text: Mineral, bone, calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D disorders
coveredTopics: Mineral, bone, calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D disorders
Interpret calcium/phosphate/PTH/ALP/25-OHD in developmental context; distinguish bone mineralization, PTH resistance, vitamin D disorders, fractures and skeletal disease.
Interpret calcium, phosphate, PTH, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, renal handling and 25-OHD together with age, nutrition, kidney function and skeletal phenotype.
Separate mineralization defects, phosphate wasting, PTH resistance, fragility and prematurity-related bone disease; one isolated vitamin D value does not establish the full mechanism.

unitMap.text: Obesity, lipids, syndromic disease, population health, and scholarship
coveredTopics: Obesity, lipids, syndromic disease, population health, and scholarship
Evaluate obesity without stigma; detect secondary/monogenic clues and metabolic comorbidity; screen/interpret lipids; apply population screening, QI, epidemiology, ethics and scholarly evidence.
Address ABP domain 14 explicitly: autoimmune polyglandular syndromes, MEN, combined endocrine disease and enteric neuroendocrine tumors (including why these are rare and specialist-led).
Add genetic dyslipidemia versus secondary lipid patterns, obesity-related metabolic complications, monogenic/syndromic obesity and undernutrition; avoid stigma and simplistic causal claims.
Population health/scholarship: screening yield and harms, bias/confounding, test performance by prevalence, consent/assent, QI measures and equitable care coordination.

topicGaps: Verified free recording time remains below the 36-hour target; exact residual is target minus uniquely identified recordings with observed runtime (currently 17.771944 hours). Scripted minutes are not media hours.

The open recording set remains thin for neonatal thyroid/newborn-screen follow-up, DSD and gender medicine, pituitary/CNS tumor syndromes, persistent hypoglycemia, calcium/phosphate/rickets, childhood dyslipidemia and genetic obesity, MEN/autoimmune polyglandular disease/enteric neuroendocrine tumors, and scholarly methods/population health.

Only one new recording was included in this expansion: the public Norton Children’s pediatric thyroid webinar. Other candidate pages without both credible topical fit and accessible observed-duration evidence were excluded; no inaccessible/member/403 file was counted.

The recorded thyroid material is general educational content and predates current guidance; use it to orient concepts, not as a contemporary clinical recommendation. Existing older recordings also require current-source reconciliation.

No complete open public teaching series covering all blueprint domains was verified in this search pass. PES member resources, listed but 403 video assets, and unavailable player recordings remain source gaps; no access control was bypassed.

American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism certification examination (only relevant to the separate adult track of the Med-Peds combined training option; out of scope for this pediatric course)
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABP Pediatric Endocrinology subspecialty certification and certifying examination exist. Certification requires applicable pediatric board eligibility plus three full-time years in an ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited pediatric endocrinology program, training verification/scholarly activity, and passing the ABP subspecialty exam. Verify current ABP admission policies directly; a course cannot confer board eligibility or certification. Boston Children’s also describes combined Medicine-Pediatrics training with Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Massachusetts General Hospital; adult Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism uses a separate ABIM pathway/examination, not a joint pediatric-endocrine board. This course is pediatric endocrinology only.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Not board eligible. Independent course completions, self-assessments and viewing hours do not satisfy ABP/RCPSC prerequisites, accredited fellowship, clinical competence, scholarly activity or exam eligibility. No guaranteed exam pass. Check current ABP policies.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet identifies two exact physician fellowship variants: Johns Hopkins Children’s Center and Boston Children’s Hospital/Harvard Medical School. Both represent the same ABP pediatric subspecialty, kept as institution variants rather than duplicated specialties. The Johns Hopkins page’s residency pathway does not substitute for checking active accreditation in ACGME ADS. Boston Children’s public overview states three years and a clinical/research split. Med-Peds joint clinical pathway is noted as an institutional combined track, not a separate board specialty; adult ABIM content/exam is outside this syllabus. This is a clinical physician fellowship, not a research-only postdoctoral listing, generic fellowship-directory label, or non-physician supplement. NIH is not added as a variant because it is outside the packet’s target institution set.
sourceCaveats: The named public institution pages verify named programs and selected structural facts, not hidden rotations, complete teaching sets, exact didactic hours, or equivalence between programs.

ACGME’s 2026 requirements index identifies a Pediatric Endocrinology requirements document effective 2026-07-01; active program accreditation for each specific site was not independently queried in ADS during this pass.

The ABP eligibility page is authoritative, current at its listed update date (2025-11-25); applicants must recheck current admission requirements. ABP currently identifies a distinct subspecialty certifying examination.
PES and Endotext pages contain both accessible and member/registration/paid materials. These are not assumed free. Some source files returned 403/bot challenge; no circumvention attempted.

The original public playlist displayed 149 videos, but this course does not claim 149 videos or count its uninspected entries. Only 34 uniquely selected playlist items with observed displayed runtime, plus two individually inspected public YouTube lectures, are counted.

No diagnosis, treatment, patient volume, institutional affiliation, guaranteed outcome, human review, accreditation, licensure or board eligibility is represented. Public real-case resources are link-only; no images or patient data are copied.

For the combined Medicine-Pediatrics option described by Boston Children’s, ABIM’s official policies confirm a separate adult Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism certification/exam; this adult track and its content remain outside the pediatric course. The packet’s Hopkins directory label “ACGME Accredited or Equivalent” is retained as a directory qualifier only; individual current accreditation was not independently verified in ADS.

The recorded thyroid material is general educational content and predates current guidance; use it to orient concepts, not as a contemporary clinical recommendation. Existing older recordings also require current-source reconciliation.

No complete open public teaching series covering all blueprint domains was verified in this search pass. PES member resources, listed but 403 video assets, and unavailable player recordings remain source gaps; no access control was bypassed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child is referred after one height measurement plots low for age. Which additional evidence most directly distinguishes a stable familial pattern from reduced linear growth velocity?

options.text: A repeat, technically reliable series of dated height measurements interpreted in the context of age and pubertal stage.
A single random growth hormone concentration.
An isolated bone-age report.
A parental report that the child is healthy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Growth is longitudinal. A repeat series permits growth-velocity interpretation; GH concentration and bone age alone are not diagnostic. This is an original educational item, not an official board question.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adolescent with acute hyperglycemia and dehydration is being evaluated for DKA. What is the safest educational next step for an independent-course learner?

options.text: Select an insulin dose from a lecture slide.
Recognize possible emergency, obtain appropriate supervised urgent evaluation, and use the current local pediatric DKA protocol.
Assume DKA based only on glucose.
Delay escalation until an outpatient antibody panel returns.

practiceQuestions.rationale: DKA is an emergency requiring qualified supervised assessment and current institution-specific protocols. This course is not an order set and does not authorize treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adolescent has irregular menses several months after menarche and an ultrasound report describes multifollicular ovaries. Which reasoning is most defensible?

options.text: Ultrasound morphology alone confirms PCOS in every adolescent.
Use adolescent-specific criteria and developmental context, assess persistent menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism, and exclude mimics; avoid premature diagnosis.
Ignore symptoms because irregular menses are always normal.
The adult Rotterdam criteria apply unchanged in all adolescents.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adolescent PCOS diagnosis is age-specific and must avoid overdiagnosis from ovarian morphology or normal early postmenarchal variation; check current guideline source.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABP 6 Disorders of Puberty (adolescent reproductive endocrine assessment)

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has short stature, slowed height velocity, weight loss and chronic abdominal symptoms. Which differential approach is best?

options.text: Consider systemic/nutritional and gastrointestinal disease as well as endocrine causes, guided by history/exam and targeted tests.
Diagnose growth hormone deficiency from short stature alone.
Assume constitutional delay without reviewing weight trajectory.
Order every endocrine test without a hypothesis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Growth impairment is nonspecific. Weight loss and chronic symptoms should keep systemic/nutritional disease in the differential; targeted context matters.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABP 4 Disorders of Growth; 17 Population Health and Screening

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has low calcium, high phosphate, and a high PTH concentration. What is an appropriate interpretation principle?

options.text: A high PTH proves primary hyperparathyroidism.
Interpret calcium-phosphate-PTH together with vitamin D, renal function, age, assay and clinical context; consider PTH resistance among differentials.
Phosphate has no value in the differential.
A low 25-hydroxyvitamin D excludes any other mineral disorder.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The combined pattern can suggest PTH resistance but is not pathognomonic; vitamin D status, renal function, age and trends matter. Clinical cases and lab values must be assessed in context.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABP 13 Disorders of Mineral and Bone Metabolism; 1 Normal Physiology

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes pediatric thyroid function testing?

options.text: TSH and thyroid hormone results should be interpreted with age, clinical context and potential assay interference.
One adult reference interval applies to neonates through adolescents.
An isolated discordant result always proves a rare receptor mutation.
Thyroid imaging replaces biochemical assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reference intervals and clinical interpretation are age- and context-dependent; discordance warrants investigation of assay/context before rare diagnoses.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABP 5 Disorders of the Thyroid Gland; 1 Normal Physiology

practiceQuestions.stem: A neonate has recurrent low glucose values after the expected transitional period. Which next educational principle is appropriate?

options.text: Assess persistence and clinical risk, obtain appropriately timed critical data under qualified care, and consider hyperinsulinism, hormone deficiencies and metabolic causes.
Assume benign transitional hypoglycemia indefinitely.
Use a home glucometer value alone to establish etiology.
Perform a fasting challenge without supervision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Persistent hypoglycemia requires context-specific, supervised evaluation; timing and laboratory-quality data are essential. No fasting procedure is authorized by this curriculum.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABP 9 Hypoglycemia; 17 Population Health and Screening

practiceQuestions.stem: Which requirement best distinguishes ACGME-accredited pediatric endocrinology fellowship from independent self-study?

options.text: 36 months of educational program with supervised clinical experiences, structured didactics, competency assessment and patient-care responsibility.
Completing 36 hours of public videos.
Passing a self-created quiz.
Accessing one institution’s program website.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME describes a 36-month program and structured supervised educational experiences; video hours do not substitute.
practiceQuestions.domain: ACGME educational requirements; ABP 18 Systems-Based Practice

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with possible DSD is referred for evaluation. Which opening communication approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use respectful, non-stigmatizing language, clarify immediate clinical priorities, protect privacy, and plan multidisciplinary evaluation with the family.
Make an irreversible conclusion from external appearance alone.
Use identity labels before asking the family how they describe the child.
Avoid discussing uncertainty.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Respectful family-centered communication, privacy, multidisciplinary consultation and an explicit account of uncertainty are essential; no single appearance determines a complete diagnosis or care plan.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABP 10 Disorders of Sex Development; 16 Gender Medicine; 18 Systems-Based Practice

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reads a seven-year-old video on pediatric PCOS and it conflicts with a recent guideline. Which action best supports safe learning?

options.text: Prefer the older lecture because it has a longer runtime.
Use the current authoritative guideline for current practice, document date/scope, and treat the older video as historical context.
Average conflicting recommendations.
Assume all open videos are current and peer-reviewed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public availability and length do not establish currency or authority. Date-check clinical sources and separate historical educational material from current recommendations.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABP 18 Systems-Based Practice; 19 Core Knowledge in Scholarly Activities
